title: The Prophet at Ta'if
hook: stoned out of the town of Ta'if, the Prophet refuses to curse its people and prays for their descendants

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, from a verse telling people who have wronged themselves not to lose hope of God's mercy. Your line was even if your sins reached the clouds.
screen: `EVEN IF YOUR SINS REACHED THE CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: A road leading away from a hill town, and a man walking it, hurt and slow. Behind him, a crowd is still shouting. He had come to Ta'if to speak to its leaders. The early biographies say they refused him, then set people along the road to jeer as he left; some tellings add stones. He reaches the shade of an orchard and sits down. This is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. What happens further down that road, as he later told it himself, is today's story.
screen: `A ROAD OUT OF A HILL TOWN.` → `STONES FROM THE ROADSIDE.` → `SHADE IN AN ORCHARD.`

segments.voice: In a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, his wife Aisha asks whether he ever faced a day harder than the battle of Uhud. He says his people had hurt him badly, and the worst was the day he went to Ibn Abd Yalil, a chief of Ta'if, and was turned away. He walked on so troubled that he only came to himself further down the road. Then the offer. He looks up and sees a cloud, and in it the angel Gabriel, who says God has heard how the people answered him, and has sent the angel of the mountains. That angel greets him and offers, if he wishes, to bring the mountains together on the town. A complete answer to everything that just happened. He says no. In paraphrase, he hopes God will bring out from their descendants people who worship God alone. Not a curse. A hope, aimed at children not yet born. The people who drove him out are left standing, and their grandchildren get a future in his words. A word on sources: the jeering crowd comes from the sira, the early biographies. The angel and the answer come from the hadith. Muslim teachers tell it as a picture of mercy at the very moment the power to answer was in his hands. He had been humiliated, he was offered the means to settle it, and he chose the longer view.
screen: `THE HARDEST DAY.` · `THE ANGEL OF THE MOUNTAINS.` · `NO: THEIR CHILDREN INSTEAD.` · `WHERE THE STORY COMES FROM.` · then, large: `NOT A CURSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person, or one group, who turned you away: a job that said no, a friend who closed the door, a family that didn't make room. Without replaying the scene, try a wish that reaches past the hurt, that things go well for them, or for the people who come after them. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own tradition's words; if you don't, just hold the wish.
Ta'if. The town that drove the Prophet out; offered the mountains against it, he gave its children a hope instead. Today's word.
Your line: not a curse. A hope, aimed at children not yet born. Day nine hundred fifty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Ta'if, from the hadith and the early biographies, as an example of the Prophet's mercy; teachers use it when speaking about answering rejection without revenge.

chat.meaning: In Bukhari's report he refused the angel of the mountains and hoped God would bring from their descendants people who worship God alone.

Ta'if.meaning: a hill town that refused the Prophet and jeered him away

Sahih al-Bukhari.meaning: a major collection of hadith, reports of the Prophet's words

Uhud.meaning: a hard battle fought near Medina in the Prophet's lifetime

Ibn Abd Yalil.meaning: a chief of Ta'if who turned the Prophet away

sira.meaning: the early biographies of the Prophet

sources.work: Sirat Rasul Allah (Ibn Ishaq, in Ibn Hisham's recension)

notes: All hadith and sira material is paraphrased; no translation quoted.

Confirm hadith numbers: Bukhari 3231 (Book of the Beginning of Creation) and Muslim 1795 for Aisha's question about a day harder than Uhud, the angel of the mountains and the Prophet's hope for their descendants.

The stoning on the road (people lined up to throw stones, bleeding feet) is from Ibn Ishaq / Ibn Hisham, not Bukhari; the script says so. The outline hook cites 'Sira; Bukhari'. Confirm wording 'blood in his sandals' is acceptable as a sira detail.
The well-known 'du'a of Ta'if' (prayer in the orchard) is deliberately left out: its chain is discussed by hadith scholars, and the script must not write or reconstruct a prayer.
Bukhari's report places the scene at 'the day of al-Aqaba' with Ibn Abd Yalil; scholars discuss whether this is the Ta'if journey itself. Script follows the common identification; Keeper to confirm.

Editor pass: the hook's 'blood in his sandals' and the stoning were softened to the jeering crowd the sira gives, with 'some tellings add stones'; the hook and fork now place the angel further down the road (Bukhari), not in the orchard.

Audit: teach no longer says Bukhari names Ta'if outright; it names Ibn Abd Yalil, a chief of Ta'if, as the hadith does. 'The people who stoned him' changed to 'drove him out' (the hook gives stones only as 'some tellings'). The older note about 'blood in his sandals' is stale: that wording is no longer in the script.
